⚠️ Closed alpha — provisional docs. OpenDefence on Kubernetes (opendefence-platform) is in closed alpha and under rapid, breaking development. This page describes a moving target and will most likely be superseded by the documentation that ships with the first public release — treat everything here as provisional, and do not rely on it for a production deployment.

This page is the map of the whole Kubernetes stack (pvarki/opendefence-platform) on one screen: which namespaces exist and what runs in them, the six-phase order everything comes up in, and how a request actually reaches a pod. Read it first; it points to where each detail in the rest of this Architecture chapter lives.

What this chapter covers

This chapter documents the Kubernetes platform core: the Kustomize manifests, PKI, ingress, service mesh, core services, data layer and observability of opendefence-platform. Product integrations (TAK, MediaMTX, Matrix, Battlelog) appear here only as a pattern — how any product namespace plugs into the core (see Integration pattern). The per-product deep dives live in their own books: TAK stack (Kubernetes), MediaMTX stack (Kubernetes) and Matrix stack (Kubernetes).

Two things deliberately stay out of this chapter:

  • The conceptual picture — what Deploy App is, the hub-and-spoke model, who talks to whom and why — is in Architecture orientation. This chapter assumes you have read it and goes straight to concrete Kubernetes resources.
  • The legacy Docker Compose stack and how it compares to this platform: see Choose your platform and the Legacy architecture chapter starting at Legacy stack overview.

Install and operations steps are also elsewhere — Deploy on Kubernetes and Day-2 operations (Kubernetes) in the Operate book.

Namespaces and workloads

The platform is a set of Kustomize components (k8s/<component>/{base,overlays/{local,cloud}}) that land in a fixed set of namespaces. The split is conventional: operator namespaces for cluster machinery, opendefence-system for the core, one app-* namespace per product.

Namespace Phase What runs there
traefik-system 1 Traefik (Helm chart 38.0.1). Entrypoint web :80 permanently redirects to websecure :443; three in-repo Yaegi plugins for callsign and client-certificate header handling. The strip-identity-headers and mTLS middleware chains also live in this namespace, though they are applied in phase 5. Local overlay runs Traefik with hostNetwork and hostPorts 80/443.
cert-manager 1–3 cert-manager v1.19.2 (phase 1), trust-manager (phase 2), and the opendefence-pki CA-chain resources (phase 3).
cnpg-system 1 CloudNativePG operator — manages every PostgreSQL cluster on the platform.
external-secrets-system 1 External Secrets Operator — generates all platform passwords in-cluster via Password generators.
linkerd 3 Linkerd control plane; its identity issuer is signed by the platform CA (identity.externalCA: true).
monitoring 4 Prometheus + Alertmanager, Loki, Alloy, kube-state-metrics and Grafana instances (the operators and CRDs arrive already in phase 1).
linkerd-viz 4 Linkerd dashboard extension, reusing the cluster Prometheus instead of running its own.
opendefence-system 5 The core: rmapi :8000, rmui (nginx UI), keycloak (serves its own TLS on hostPort :9443), the keycloak-init realm-import Job, openldap :1389/:1636, CNPG clusters rmapi-postgres and keycloak-postgres, and the mtls-optional / mtls-strict TLSOptions.
app-tak 6 tak-server pod — TAK split into five JVM services plus an nginx UI and the takrmapi integration API :8003 — with CNPG tak-postgres (PostGIS).
app-mtx 6 mtx-server pod — mediamtx plus nginx UI and mtxrmapi :8005 — with CNPG mtx-postgres.
app-matrix 6 matrix pod — Synapse :8008 (federation disabled), Matrix Authentication Service, LiveKit SFU, the matrix-rtc JWT service, nginx UI and matrixrmapi :8012 — with CNPG matrix-postgres and mas-postgres.
app-battlelog 6 battlelog (blapi :3000, the one workload not in the mesh) with CNPG battlelog-postgres (PostGIS). The simplest product shape.

Keycloak is intentionally missing an edge from Traefik — clients reach it directly at kc.<domain>:9443 (see the entry-path diagram further down).

The phase model

There is no GitOps controller — deployment is an ordered pipeline of six Kustomize phases driven by the task runner (mechanics in Deployment model). The order exists because later phases consume CRDs, webhooks and certificates that earlier phases create. The six phases:

blocks.html:
1. **infra-phase1** installs the operator layer: CloudNativePG, External Secrets Operator, cert-manager, Traefik (with its CRDs) and the Prometheus/Grafana operators — everything that defines CRDs other phases will instantiate.
  2. **infra-phase2** adds trust-manager (which will distribute the CA bundle to every namespace) and the callsign secret mirror; the cloud overlay also creates the Let's Encrypt ClusterIssuers.
  3. **infra-phase3** builds the platform PKI (self-signed root → intermediate → issuing ClusterIssuers, detailed in PKI & trust) and installs Linkerd, whose identity issuer is signed by that same CA.
  4. **monitoring** instantiates what the phase-1 operators made possible: Prometheus and Alertmanager CRs, Loki, Alloy, Grafana and linkerd-viz — see Observability pipeline.
  5. **opendefence** deploys the core itself — the mTLS middleware chains plus rmapi, rmui, Keycloak, OpenLDAP and the two core CNPG clusters.
  6. **opendefence-apps** deploys the four product namespaces, each following the integration pattern.

Between phases, the pipeline blocks on kubectl rollout status gates so a phase never runs against a half-ready predecessor — the gate table is in Deployment model. One deliberate wrinkle crosses the phases: Traefik (phase 1) requires a callsign shared secret that is only generated in phase 5, and the gap converges through External Secrets reconciliation — see Data & secrets.

One request, end to end

Traffic enters the cluster on three distinct paths — only the first one gets Traefik's middleware treatment:

own TLS, client-auth=request"] raw["Raw TCP/UDP Services
NodePort local / LoadBalancer cloud"] end web["HTTP(S) backends: rmui, rmapi,
product UIs and APIs, Synapse,
MAS, matrix-rtc, Grafana"] kcpod["Keycloak pod"] takp["TAK: 8089, 8443,
8090-8094, 9000-9002"] mtxp["MediaMTX: 1936, 8322, 8890,

blocks.html:
The second path is Keycloak's own TLS (its image is built with client-auth=request); Linkerd treats 9443 as an opaque port and passes it through as raw TCP. The third path is the product protocols that are not HTTP at all — TAK CoT streaming and federation, MediaMTX media protocols, LiveKit TURN/media — exposed as NodePorts locally and as LoadBalancer services in the cloud, bypassing Traefik entirely. Details and the full FQDN/port table are in Ingress & network edge.

For the main path, here is what happens to one HTTPS request, say https://mtls.<domain>/api/...:

  1. TLS terminates at Traefik on the websecure :443 entrypoint. The route's TLSOption decides optional vs strict client-certificate policy per host; presented certificates are verified against the platform ca-bundle.
  2. Identity headers are scrubbed. strip-identity-headers runs as a default entrypoint middleware, so before any routing logic all client-suppliable identity headers are stripped. Nothing downstream can be fed a spoofed identity.
  3. The callsign is checked. On mTLS routes the mtls-chain middleware validates the verified certificate CN against rmapi and stamps trusted Callsign* headers; an invalid callsign is redirected or rejected. Full walkthrough, header list and per-host TLSOption map in Edge mTLS & callsign checks.
  4. The request enters the pod. Traefik forwards plain HTTP to the backend Service. Traefik itself is not meshed, but the destination pod is Linkerd-injected: the connection lands on the pod's sidecar proxy, which hands it to the application container as plain HTTP on localhost.
  5. Inside the mesh, hops are mTLS again. Any follow-up in-cluster call — a product API calling rmapi:8000, rmapi calling a product's integration API — is written as plain HTTP but transparently wrapped in Linkerd mutual TLS, and callers pin the expected peer by its Linkerd identity CN. How identity is issued and verified is covered in Service mesh (Linkerd).

Reading guide

The rest of the chapter, in a sensible reading order:

  • Deployment model — the Kustomize/component layout, the phase pipeline in depth, the task runner, kind vs k3s environments, Zarf packaging (online and air-gapped) and CalVer releases.
  • PKI & trust — the self-signed root → intermediate CA chain, the trust-manager ca-bundle that reaches every namespace, Let's Encrypt for public certificates, and per-user client certificates minted through cert-manager.
  • Ingress & network edge — Traefik configuration, the hostname map (<domain>, mtls., per-product hosts), middleware wiring, and the raw TCP/UDP exposure for TAK, MediaMTX and LiveKit.
  • Edge mTLS & callsign checks — TLSOptions, the three Yaegi plugins, the callsign validity/redirect chain, and the current revocation stance (OCSP disabled; the validity check is the interim enforcement).
  • Service mesh (Linkerd) — external-CA identity, which workloads are injected (and that battlelog is not), opaque ports, and identity pinning between rmapi and the product APIs.
  • Core services — rmapi, rmui, Keycloak (and the keycloak-init realm import), OpenLDAP, and the core databases in opendefence-system.
  • Integration pattern — the anatomy of a product namespace: the kraftwerk-init.json contract in both directions, healthchecks, secrets and the per-product database.
  • Data & secrets — all seven CNPG clusters (each instances: 1, no backups configured), the ESO password generators, and the cross-namespace secret-mirror pattern.
  • Observability pipeline — Prometheus operator wiring, Loki + Alloy log collection, Grafana, and linkerd-viz.
